definitions.text: See Wax insect, under Wax.
The covering, or coat, of a mammal, whether of wool, fur, or hair.
Of or pertaining to the sea; marine; pelagic; as, pelagian shells.

A follower of Pelagius, a British monk, born in the later part of the 4th century, who denied the doctrines of hereditary sin, of the connection between sin and death, and of conversion through grace.
Of or pertaining to Pelagius, or to his doctrines.
The doctrines of Pelagius.
Of or pertaining to the ocean; -- applied especially to animals that live at the surface of the ocean, away from the coast.
Pertaining to, or designating, an organic acid (called also nonoic acid) found in the leaves of the geranium (Pelargonium) and allied plants.

A large genus of plants of the order Geraniaceæ, differing from Geranium in having a spurred calyx and an irregular corolla. them natives of South Africa, and many having very beautiful blossoms. See the Note under Geranium.
Of or pertaining to the Pelasgians, an ancient people of Greece, of roving habits.
(Zoöl.)
Wandering.
Of or pertaining to the Pelasgians, an ancient people of Greece, of roving habits.
(Zoöl.)
Wandering.

Glass threads or fibers formed by the wind from bits blown from frothy lava or from the tips of lava jets or from bits of liquid lava thrown into the air. It often collects in thick masses resembling tow.
See Pelican.
Those birds that are related to the pelican; the Totipalmi.

A figure, somewhat hatched-shaped, bounded by a semicircle and two inverted quadrants, and equal in area to the square ABCD inclosed by the chords of the four quadrants. [Written also pelicoid.] Math. Dict.
Same as Lamellibranchia.
See Peregrine. [Obs.]
A woman's cape; especially, a fur cape that is longer in front than behind.

Money; riches; lucre; gain; -- generally conveying the idea of something ill-gotten or worthless. It has no plural. "Mucky pelf." Spenser. "Paltry pelf." Burke. Can their pelf prosper, not got by valor or industry Fuller.
Of or pertaining to pelf. Stanyhurst.
Pelf; also, figuratively, rubbish; trash. [Obs.] Cranmer.
Pelf; also, figuratively, rubbish; trash. [Obs.] Cranmer.
(Zoöl.)

Any large webfooted bird of the genus of Pelecanus, of which about a dozen species are known. They have an enormous bill, to the lower edge of which is attached a pouch in which captured fishes are temporarily stored. brown species (P. fuscus) are abundant on the Florida coast in winter, but breed about the lakes in the Rocky Mountains and British America.
(Old Chem.)

A retort or still having a curved tube or tubes leading back from the head to the body for continuous condensation and redistillation. distilling apparatus. Frigate pelican (Zoöl.), the frigate bird. See under Frigate. the order Lyomeri, remarkable for the enormous development of the jaws, which support a large gular pouch. blossom of a climbing plant (Aristolochia grandiflora) of the West Indies; also, the plant itself. leucocephalus). The head and throat are destitute of feathers; the plumage is white, with the quills and the tail greenish black. representation of a pelican in the act of wounding her breast in order to nourish her young with her blood; -- a practice fabulously attributed to the bird, on account of which it was adopted as a symbol of the Redeemer, and of charity. Aporrhais, esp. Aporrhais pes-pelicani of Europe.
Louisiana; -- a nickname alluding to the device on its seal.
The American coot (Fulica).
See Pelecoid.
A suborder of Theromorpha, including terrestrial reptiles from the Permian formation.
A variety of iolite, of a smoky blue color; pelioma.
(Med.)
A livid ecchymosis.
(Min.)
See Peliom.
An outer garment for men or women, originally of fur, or lined with fur; a lady's outer garment, made of silk or other fabric.
To pelt; to knock about. [Obs.] Holland.
A skin or hide; a pelt.
A roll of parchment; a parchment record. Clerk of the pells, formerly, an officer of the exchequer who entered accounts on certain parchment rolls, called pell rolls. [Eng.]
A porpoise.
A customs duty on skins of leather.
An erythematous affection of the skin, with severe constitutional and nervous symptoms, endemic in Northern Italy.
One who is afficted with pellagra. Chambers's Encyc.
Pertaining to, or affected with, or attendant on, pellagra; as, pellagrous insanity.
A little ball; as, a pellet of wax .
A bullet; a ball for firearms. [Obs.] Bacon. As swift as a pellet out of a gun. Chaucer. Pellet molding (Arch.), a narrow band ornamented with smalt, flat disks.
To form into small balls. [Obs.] Shak.
Made of, or like, pellets; furnished with pellets. [R.] "This pelleted storm." Shak.
A division of Nudibranchiata, in which the mantle itself serves as a gill.
A thin skin or film.
(Chem.)
A thin film formed on the surface of an evaporating solution.
Of or pertaining to a pellicle. Henslow.
The redshank; -- so called from its note. [Prov. Eng.]

The common name of the several species of the genus Parietaria, low, harmless weeds of the Nettle family; -- also called wall pellitory, and lichwort. P.Pennsylvanica is found in the United States; and six or seven more species are found near the Mediterranean, or in the Orient.
See Pall-mall.
In utter confusion; with confused violence. "Men, horses, chariots, crowded pellmell." Milton.
Transparent; clear; limpid; translucent; not opaque. "Pellucid crystal." Dr. H. More. "Pellucid streams." Wordsworth.
The quality or state of being pellucid; transparency; translucency; clearness; as, the pellucidity of the air. Locke.
In a pellucid manner.
The quality or state of being pellucid; transparency; translucency; clearness; as, the pellucidity of the air. Locke.
The under surface of the foot.
A supposed new metal found in columbite, afterwards shown to be identical with columbium, or niobium.
Of or pertaining to the Peloponnesus, or southern peninsula of Greece.
A native or an inhabitant of the Peloponnesus.
Abnormal regularity; the state of certain flowers, which, being naturally irregular, have become regular through a symmetrical repetition of the special irregularity.
Abnormally regular or symmetrical. Darwin.
An instrument similar to a mariner's compass, but without magnetic needles, and having two sight vanes by which bearings are taken, esp. such as cannot be taken by the compass.
A Basque, Spanish, and Spanish-American game played in a court, in which a ball is struck with a wickerwork racket.
Packs or bales of Spanish wool.

The skin of a beast with the hair on; a raw or undressed hide; a skin preserved with the hairy or woolly covering on it. See 4th Fell. Sir T. Browne. Raw pelts clapped about them for their clothes. Fuller.
The human skin. [Jocose] Dryden.
(Falconry)
The body of any quarry killed by the hawk. Pelt rot, a disease affecting the hair or wool of a beast.
To strike with something thrown or driven; to assail with pellets or missiles, as, to pelt with stones; pelted with hail. The children billows seem to pelt the clouds. Shak.
To throw; to use as a missile. My Phillis me with pelted apples plies. Dryden.
To throw missiles. Shak.
To throw out words. [Obs.] Another smothered seems to peltand swear. Shak.
A blow or stroke from something thrown.
(Antiq.)
A small shield, especially one of an approximately elliptic form, or crescent-shaped.
(Bot.)
A flat apothecium having no rim.
Shield-shaped; scutiform; (Bot.) having the stem or support attached to the lower surface, instead of at the base or margin; -- said of a leaf or other organ.
Shield-shaped; scutiform; (Bot.) having the stem or support attached to the lower surface, instead of at the base or margin; -- said of a leaf or other organ.
One who pelts.
A pinchpenny; a mean, sordid person; a miser; a skinflint.
A cross formed of two strips of different metals, to illustrate the Peltier effect.

The production or absorption of heat at the junction of two metals on the passage of a current. Heat generated by the passage of the current in one direction will be absorbed if the current is reversed.
Shieldlike, with the outline nearly circular; peltate. Henslow.
Mean; paltry. [Obs.] Shak.

A form of impulse turbine or water wheel, consisting of a row of double cup-shaped buckets arranged round the rim of a wheel and actuated by one or more jets of water playing into the cups at high velocity.
Pelts or skins, collectively; skins with the fur on them; furs.
Peltry. [Obs.]
The South American hairy armadillo (Dasypus villosus).
A crisp, hard, thin paper, sometimes used for postage stamps.
Of or pertaining to Pelusium, an ancient city of Egypt; as, the Pelusiac (or former eastern) outlet of the Nile.

Of, pertaining to, or in the region of, the pelvis; as, pelvic cellulitis. Pelvic arch, or Pelvic girdle (Anat.), the two or more bony or cartilaginous pieces of the vertebrate skeleton to which the hind limbs are articulated. When fully ossified, the arch usually consists of three principal bones on each side, the ilium, ischium, and pubis, which are often closely united in the adult, forming the innominate bone. See Innominate bone, under Innominate.
An instrument for measuring the dimensions of the pelvis. Coxe.
The measurement of the pelvis.
(Anat.)
The pelvic arch, or the pelvic arch together with the sacrum. See Pelvic arch, under Pelvic, and Sacrum.
(Zoöl.)
The calyx of a crinoid. Pelvis of the kidney (Anat.), the basinlike cavity into which the ureter expands as it joins the kidney.
